Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)  
● Leading cause of death worldwide  
● Over 30% of Americans over 35 die from IHD  
● Caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium)  
Ischemia  
● Not just a drop in oxygen supply (hypoxia), but also a decrease in nutrient delivery and waste removal due  
to reduced blood flow  
Coronary Arteries  
● Left Coronary Artery (LCA): Branches into the left circumflex artery (LCX) and the left anterior  
descending artery (LAD)  
● Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Includes branches such as the posterior descending artery (PDA)  
Blood Supply Areas  
● LAD: Supplies 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the anterior wall of the left ventricle.  
● LCX: Supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle.  
● RCA and PDA: Supply the right ventricular wall and part of the posterior wall of the septum, as well as the  
posterior inferior wall of the left ventricle  
Causes of Ischemic Heart Disease  
● Atherosclerosis: The primary cause, responsible for over 90% of cases. Involves the formation of  
lipid-based plaques under the endothelium, creating blockages.  
○ Stable Plaques: Have a cap and cause stable angina, a type of chest pain that resolves with rest or  
vasodilators.  
○ Unstable Plaques: Can rupture, leading to platelet accumulation and thrombus formation, causing  
acute coronary syndromes like unstable angina and MI.  
Types of Angina  
● Stable Angina: Caused by stable plaques. Chest pain resolves with rest or vasodilators (Nitroglycerine)  
● Unstable Angina: Caused by unstable plaques. Chest pain may not resolve with rest or vasodilators and can  
progress to MI.  
● Prinzmetal or Variant Angina: Caused by transient vasospasm. Chest pain resolves with vasodilators.  
Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)  
● Includes unstable angina and myocardial infarction (MI).  
● NSTEMI (Non-ST Elevated Myocardial Infarction): Involves subendocardial infarction.  
● STEMI (ST Elevated Myocardial Infarction): Involves transmural infarction.  
Diagnosing MI with ECG  
● ECG Leads and Infarction Location:  
○ V1 to V4: Anterior wall infarction (LAD occlusion).  
○ V5, V6, AVL, and lead I: Lateral wall infarction (left circumflex artery).  
○ Leads III, AVF, and II: Inferior wall infarction (RCA or PDA).  
Hrach Vardanyan | 3  
ECG Changes in MI  
● NSTEMI: ST depression. non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction  
● STEMI: ST elevation. ST-elevation myocardial infarction  
Troponin  
● Elevated for more than 0.04 troponin levels indicate myocardial cell death, as troponin is released when  
the myocardium starts to die  
Troponin I - Normal Range: Less than 0.04 ng/mL (nanograms per milliliter)  
Troponin T - Normal Range: Less than 0.01 ng/mL  
Other Causes of Ischemic Heart Disease  
● Vasospasm: Can cause transient or severe, long-term vasospasm leading to MI.  
● Microvascular Dysfunction: Affects smaller blood vessels, potentially leading to conditions like  
Takotsubo myopathy (broken heart syndrome).  
Myocardial Infarction  
Causes  
● Hyperlipidemia: Leads to atherosclerosis, with fats depositing on the walls of arteries.  
● Deep Venous Thrombosis (Thrombophlebitis)  
● Diabetes Mellitus  
● Metabolic Syndrome: Characterized by a high BMI.  
● Obesity  
● Hypertension  
Symptoms of MI  
● Chest pain (squeezing, choking chest pain)  
● Shortness of breath (SOB)  
● Dyspnea  
● Hypoxia  
● Nausea  
● Vomiting  
● Epigastric pain  
Nitroglycerine Precautions  
● Always keep nitroglycerine in a black bottle in a dark place; do not store it in the car.  
● Common side effect: headache (an expected effect).  
● As a vasodilator, nitroglycerine can cause hypotension, leading to orthostatic hypotension.  
● It is recommended to lie down when taking nitroglycerine sublingually.  
● Forms: sublingual tablets, patch (apply with gloves), cream (apply on the arm), and IV.  
● Always monitor blood pressure when taking nitroglycerine.  
Myocardial Infarction (MI)  
● MI is an acute condition resulting in irreversible necrosis of the heart muscle.  
● After an MI, it is crucial to monitor the patient to prevent another MI.

Stable Angina  
● Stable angina can be a chronic condition.  
● Recommendations: stop smoking, lose weight, avoid fatty foods and alcohol, and use nitroglycerine to  
control chest pain.  
● Triggers: exercise, physical work, unhealthy food, alcohol, and immobilization.  
● Chest pain protocol:  
○ Take the first dose of nitroglycerine while lying down. (If the pain does not subside after the first  
dose, call 911. The second and third doses provide an additional 10 minutes for emergency services  
to arrive)  
○ If pain persists after 5 minutes, take a second dose.  
○ If pain still persists, take a third dose (maximum of 3 doses, 5 minutes apart).  
● Signs of stable angina turning unstable: nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and dyspepsia (early symptoms  
of MI, not to be confused with gastrointestinal issues).  
Hospital Protocol for Suspected MI  
1. Initial Actions:  
● Connect the patient to a peripheral device and EKG (to check for STEMI or NSTEMI).  
● Draw blood for lab tests: check D-Dimer, aPTT (coagulation panel), and troponin levels (troponin levels  
above 0.04 indicate MI. Troponin I - Normal Range: Less than 0.04 ng/mL Troponin T - Normal  
Range: Less than 0.01 ng/mL)  
a) Coagulation panel  
i)  
Prothrombin Time (PT): Measures the time it takes for blood to clot. It evaluates the  
extrinsic pathway and common pathway of coagulation.  
ii)  
International Normalized Ratio (INR): Standardizes the PT results regardless of testing  
methods, making it easier to compare results across different labs.  
iii)  
iv)  
v)  
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT): Measures the time it takes for blood to  
clot, focusing on the intrinsic pathway and common pathway of coagulation.  
Thrombin Time (TT): Measures the time it takes for a clot to form in the presence of  
thrombin, evaluating the final step of the coagulation process.  
Fibrinogen Level: Assesses the amount of fibrinogen, a protein essential for blood clot  
formation.  
vi)  
D-Dimer: A test that helps diagnose clotting disorders, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT)  
and pulmonary embolism, by measuring the presence of fibrin degradation products.  
● Look for ST segment elevation  
2. First Treatment:  
● Administer Aspirin (suspected MI patients should take an emergency chewable Aspirin 160 mg - 2 baby  
doses)  
MONA Protocol for MI  
● Morphine: For severe chest pain radiating to the jaw, left shoulder, back, and epigastric area. Assess the  
severity of the pain (MI pain scale is 8-10; pain less than 5 is unlikely to be MI).  
● Oxygen: For shortness of breath (SOB) and hypoxia.  
● Nitroglycerine: To dilate blood vessels.  
● Aspirin: To reduce the risk of thrombus formation.  
● Additional medications: Heparin (anticoagulant) or Enoxaparin (to prevent further clot damage).

Symptoms  
Symptoms of stable angina are predictable and occur in a  
pattern, often triggered by similar activities and relieved by  
rest or medication.  
Signs of stable angina turning unstable:  
nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and  
dyspepsia (indigestion) (early symptoms of  
MI, not to be confused with gastrointestinal  
issues).  
Chest Pain or Discomfort:  
● Typically feels like pressure, squeezing, or fullness  
in the chest.  
● Often triggered by physical exertion, stress, or cold  
weather.  
● Usually lasts a few minutes and goes away with  
rest or medication (such as nitroglycerin).  
Pain Radiating to Other Areas: Pain can spread to the  
arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, or back. Pain usually lasts for a  
few minutes (typically less than 10 minutes).  
Shortness of Breath: Difficulty breathing during physical  
activity or stress.  
Note  
Fatigue: Feeling unusually tired during or after physical  
activity.  
Nausea: Sometimes accompanied by feelings of nausea or  
lightheadedness.  
Sweating: Cold, clammy skin.

Variant Angina / Prinzmetal's angina  
Treatment  
Condition/Cause  
Monitor  
Coronary arteries experience temporary spasms,  
narrowing the arteries. These spasms restrict  
blood flow to the heart, causing chest pain,  
typically at rest and often during early morning.  
Note  
Complications  
Differentiate  
Symptoms  
● Occurs at rest, often during the  
night or early morning.  
● Caused by coronary artery  
spasm.  
Chest Pain: Occurs at rest, often during the  
night or early morning. Can be severe and  
feels like pressure, squeezing, or tightness in  
the chest.  
● Not typically triggered by  
exertion or stress.  
Pain Radiating to Other Areas: Pain can  
spread to the arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, or  
back. Pain typically lasts for a few minutes.  
Shortness of Breath: Difficulty breathing  
during an angina attack.  
● Responds to calcium channel  
blockers and nitrates.  
● Pain typically lasts for a few  
minutes.  
Nausea: Feeling sick to the stomach, which  
may be accompanied by vomiting.  
Sweating: Cold, clammy skin.  
Palpitations: Feeling of a rapid or irregular  
heartbeat.
